issues.legal_issue: Delay that remains within the limitation period does not, by itself, justify refusing specific performance where it has caused no third-party rights, waiver, or inequity.
material_facts: The contract required the sale deed to be executed within five months, and the suit was filed within the applicable limitation period.
The suit was filed nine months after the last notice, not more than a year later as the High Court had assumed.
The Court found no acquisition of rights by third parties and no waiver or other inequity arising from the delay.
issues.conclusion: The delay did not justify denying specific performance.
issues.legal_principle: In a specific-performance suit, delay beyond the limitation period is relevant; delay within that period may also matter if third parties acquire rights or if waiver or inequity results. In the absence of those circumstances, delay alone does not warrant refusal of discretionary relief. No earlier case was cited for this point.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and suit_within_limitation and no_third_party_rights_from_delay and no_waiver_or_inequity_from_delay

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract for sale.
predicates.suit_within_limitation: The claimant filed the suit within the applicable limitation period.
predicates.no_third_party_rights_from_delay: No third party acquired rights in the subject matter because of the delay.
predicates.no_waiver_or_inequity_from_delay: The delay did not result in waiver or make the requested relief inequitable in the circumstances.

issues.definition: When a claimant brings a timely specific-performance suit and the delay has caused neither third-party rights nor waiver or inequity, the delay alone does not justify refusing specific performance.

issues.legal_issue: Readiness and willingness in a specific-performance suit may be shown by the substance of the plaint as a whole and the evidence, without prescribed wording or a specific formula.
material_facts: The claimant paid two-thirds of the consideration when the written agreement was executed, leaving only the balance to be paid.
The plaint, read as a whole, stated that the claimant demanded that the seller accept the balance and execute the sale deed.
The claimant and another witness gave evidence in support of readiness and willingness.
The claimant had deposited the balance pursuant to the trial court's decree.
issues.conclusion: The plaint and evidence sufficiently established the claimant's readiness and willingness to perform his obligations.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires the plaintiff to aver and prove that he has performed, or has always been and is willing to perform, the essential terms of the contract. No specific phraseology or form is required if the plaint as a whole conveys that substance, and readiness and willingness are assessed from the relevant facts and conduct. The Court relied on Ramesh Chandra Chandiok v. Chuni Lal Sabharwal and the three-Judge decision in Syed Dastagir v. T.R. Gopalakrishna Setty. It distinguished Ouseph Varghese v. Joseph Aley and Abdul Khader Rowther v. P.K. Sara Bai, which concerned different pleading circumstances.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and plaint_as_whole_indicates_willingness and claimant_demanded_contractual_performance and evidence_supports_readiness and claimant_paid_substantial_consideration

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract for sale.
predicates.plaint_as_whole_indicates_willingness: The claimant's plaint, read as a whole, described willingness to perform the claimant's contractual obligations.
predicates.claimant_demanded_contractual_performanc: The claimant asked the other contracting party to accept the balance consideration and complete the sale.
predicates.evidence_supports_readiness: The claimant presented evidence supporting readiness and willingness to perform.
predicates.claimant_paid_substantial_consideration: The claimant had paid a substantial part of the agreed consideration before seeking completion of the contract.

issues.definition: In a specific-performance suit, when the plaint as a whole conveys willingness, the claimant demanded completion, evidence supports readiness, and substantial consideration was paid, the readiness-and-willingness requirement is satisfied without prescribed wording.

issues.legal_issue: A claim for compensation as alternative relief does not preclude a claimant from obtaining specific performance.
material_facts: The claimant sought specific performance and also claimed compensation in the alternative.
issues.conclusion: The alternative claim for compensation did not bar specific performance.
issues.legal_principle: Section 21 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 permits a claim for compensation in a suit for specific performance. Making that claim in the alternative does not disentitle the claimant to the principal relief of specific performance. No earlier case was cited for this point.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract for sale.
predicates.compensation_claimed_as_alternative_reli: The claimant requested compensation as an alternative to specific performance.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks specific performance and requests compensation as an alternative, the alternative compensation claim does not bar specific performance.

issues.legal_issue: The purchaser's conduct does not disentitle the purchaser to specific performance merely because the purchaser's spouse occupied the property as a tenant or the seller denied executing the agreement.
material_facts: The seller denied executing the agreement, but the trial court found that the seller had executed it, and the High Court confirmed that finding.
The purchaser's wife was a tenant in the property, and the seller's representatives argued that the purchaser's conduct in bringing the agreement into existence weighed against discretionary relief.
The purchaser had paid two-thirds of the consideration, and payment of the balance was the remaining obligation.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser's alleged conduct did not disentitle him to specific performance.
issues.legal_principle: Whether a party was ready and willing, and whether the party's conduct warrants refusing discretionary relief, is assessed from the entirety of the relevant facts and circumstances rather than by a rigid formula. The Court relied on the approach to conduct and readiness and willingness in Ramesh Chandra Chandiok v. Chuni Lal Sabharwal and Syed Dastagir v. T.R. Gopalakrishna Setty.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and agreement_execution_found and purchaser_paid_substantial_consideration and only_balance_performance_remained

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract for sale.
predicates.agreement_execution_found: The court found that the seller executed the agreement, despite the seller's denial.
predicates.purchaser_paid_substantial_consideration: The purchaser had paid a substantial part of the agreed consideration.
predicates.only_balance_performance_remained: The purchaser's remaining contractual obligation was payment of the balance consideration.

issues.definition: When execution of the agreement is found, the purchaser has paid substantial consideration, and only the balance remains to be performed, the purchaser's alleged conduct does not by itself disentitle the purchaser to specific performance.
